sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Brokkr** (*brokkr*) — Dwarf Smith · Badger, panting — is the smith who took the strangest wager in the northern corpus: his craft against Loki's head. While his brother worked the forge, Brokkr worked the bellows through three castings — the golden-bristled boar Gullinbursti, the drip-gold ring Draupnir, and the hammer Mjǫllnir — and the Æsir judged the last of them the best treasure ever made.[^1]

Old Norse *Brokkr* is attested only in Snorri's Prose Edda, where the episode of the wager is told in Skáldskaparmál with a smith's precision: what was laid in the fire, what came out, and what each interruption cost. Beside the proper name stands the common noun *brokkr*, 'a badger', and whether the dwarf carried the animal-name or a separate formation is unsettled in the handbooks.[^2] His brother at the forge is named Eitri in the main text of the Prose Edda; some manuscripts read Sindri, and the reference works register both.[^3]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Brokkr** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name; the mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2. The temple is domain-less: the plain-ASCII brokkr.com is held outside the collection and watched for release, and no form of the name is claimed here.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 35 (the wager of the head and the making of the three treasures), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. brokkr.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Brokk, Eitri, Sindri.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in normalized Old Norse as **Brokkr** (nominative; genitive *Brokks*). It is a strong masculine with the nominative ending *-r* and a geminate -kk- that the spelling records faithfully; the ASCII fallback *brokkr* loses nothing but the capital, which is precisely why the name is Tier 2 under the mechanical rule.[^1]

The etymology is an honest open question. Cleasby–Vigfusson gloss the common noun *brokkr* 'a badger' (comparing Danish *brok*), and the dictionaries note figurative senses; the traditional glosses carried by the lexicon — 'badger, panting' — reflect this noun and the older suggestion of a connection with heavy breathing. Whether the dwarf's name is the animal-name, a byname turned proper name, or a separate formation is unsettled: Simek registers the obscurity rather than settling it, and so does this temple.[^2]

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **b** → **B** — Same, capitalized
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same

The project holds no domain for this name: brokkr.com was registered in the ordinary way outside the collection and is watched for release.

sources.citation: Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. brokkr.
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. brokkr; Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993), s.v. Brokk.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈbrok.kr̩/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Br-** — Voiced bilabial stop [b] into a trilled [r]; stress on the first syllable, as in every Old Norse word
- **-o-** — A short open back vowel [ɔ]-[o]; the manuscripts write a plain short o, and the Younger Futhark would carve it with the úr-rune
- **-kkr** — A true geminate [kː], the doubled k held long across the syllable boundary, closing into the syllabic nominative [r̩]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'BROK-ur' — two beats, the o short as in *lot*, the double k held a moment longer than English allows.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Brokkr, the dwarf of Skáldskaparmál; beside it the common noun brokkr, 'a badger'
- **Younger Futhark** — ᛒᚱᚢᚴᛦ, the Viking-Age runic rendering (b-r-u-k-R)
- **Companion name** — Eitri, the brother at the forge; some manuscripts read Sindri

Brokkr is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses: the name is already plain ASCII, and the tier rule is a report on orthography, not on the smith.[^1]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and orthography.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Brokkr** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th–14th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister codices, recording material generations older.[^1] Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the younger futhark; no runic attestation of this name survives, so the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a strong masculine: stem *Brokk-* with the nominative singular ending *-r*.
- The geminate -kk- is a true long consonant, held across the syllable boundary; the manuscripts write it double, and the spelling is exact.
- In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᚱᚢᚴᛦ (b-r-u-k-R), with úr writing the o and ᛦ the final nominative -r.
- The Unicode restoration Brokkr loses nothing to ASCII but the capital: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII, which is why the name stands in Tier 2 — an orthographic report, not a judgment on the smith.[^2]

sources.citation: Faulkes, Anthony, ed., Edda: Prologue and Gylfaginning (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1982), on the manuscript witnesses.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Brokkr** is catalogued under the domain Dwarf Smith — and the corpus earns the label in a single afternoon's work: three castings, three treasures, and a wager collected to its letter.[^1]

### The Smith of the Wager

When [[loki|Loki]] boasted that no dwarf could match the sons of Ívaldi's treasures, Brokkr staked the boast against Loki's head — and won. His is the only smith in the corpus whose skill is proved in open competition.

### The Bellows

His own station was the bellows: the unbroken breath that held each heat. Twice a fly's sting failed to move him; the third sting, on the eyelid, cost the hammer its handle — the one flaw sabotage ever bought from him.

### The Three Treasures

Gullinbursti for [[freyr|Freyr]], Draupnir for [[odinn|Óðinn]], Mjǫllnir for [[thor|Þórr]]: the boar that outruns horses, the ring that drips eight rings every ninth night, the hammer that never misses. Every one remains a working tool of the gods through the rest of the corpus.

### The Letter of the Bargain

When Loki pleaded that the head was staked but not the neck, Brokkr honored the reading — and sewed the trickster's lips shut with the thread called Vartari. Craft, patience, and a lawyer's precision in one figure.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 35, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
Brokkr's iconography is the iconography of his episode — the corpus gives him no cult regalia, but the wager fixed a small set of objects no retelling can omit:[^1]

- **The bellows** — his station in the forge: the unbroken breath on which every casting depended, and the one duty the wager allowed no rest from
- **The fly** — the small sabotage aimed at the work rather than the worker: twice it failed, and at the last it bought only a shortened handle
- **Mjǫllnir's short handle** — the honest flaw in the perfect weapon; the Æsir judged the marred hammer best of all the treasures all the same
- **The awl and the thread Vartari** — the instruments of the bargain's enforcement: the head won, the neck denied, and the price taken another way
- **The head as stake** — the highest wager the corpus records: a trickster's life against a smith's confidence[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 35, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Brokk, Mjǫllnir.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Brokkr's mythology is a single, perfectly shaped narrative — the wager of the head — preceded by the mischief that made it necessary and closed by the loophole that shaped its price.[^1]

### The Hair of Gold and the Sons of Ívaldi (Skáldskaparmál 35)

[[loki|Loki]] cut off all the hair of [[sif|Sif]], [[thor|Þórr]]'s wife, for a prank; Þórr caught him and was set to break every bone when Loki swore to have the svartálfar make hair of gold that would grow like other hair. He went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ívaldi, who made the hair, the ship Skíðblaðnir, and the spear Gungnir. Grímnismál keeps the ship's making in verse: 'Ívaldi's sons went in days of old to make Skíðblaðnir, best of ships, for bright [[freyr|Freyr]].'[^1][^2]

### The Wager of the Head (Skáldskaparmál 35)

On his way home Loki stopped at Brokkr's forge and wagered his own head that Brokkr's brother could not make three treasures as good. Snorri names the brother Eitri; some manuscripts read [[sindri|Sindri]], and the handbooks register both. The terms placed Brokkr at the bellows: the breath was not to falter until each work came out of the fire.[^1][^3]

### Three Castings, Three Stings

A pig's skin went in first, and a fly stung Brokkr's hand; he blew on, and out came the boar Gullinbursti, bristles of gold. Gold went in next; the fly stung his neck twice as hard; he blew on, and out came Draupnir. Iron went in last, with Eitri's warning that all would be spoiled if the blast faltered now; the fly stung between his eyes until blood ran into one eye, Brokkr swept it away and paused the bellows for an instant — and the hammer came out with a short handle. The story never names the fly; it never needs to.[^1]

### The Judgment of the Æsir

At Ásgarðr, [[odinn|Óðinn]], Þórr, and Freyr judged. Loki gave Gungnir to Óðinn, the hair to Þórr for Sif, Skíðblaðnir to Freyr. Brokkr gave Gullinbursti to Freyr — running through air and water better than any horse, its bristles lighting the dark — Draupnir to Óðinn, dripping eight rings of equal weight every ninth night, and Mjǫllnir to Þórr: unerring, returning to the hand, small enough to hide in the shirt, flawed only in the handle. The judgment was that the hammer was best of all, the greatest defense against the rime-giants. Loki owed his head.[^1]

### The Head and the Neck

Loki offered ransom; Brokkr refused all gold. Loki fled on his sky-shoes; Þórr caught him at Brokkr's request. Then the letter of the bargain: the head was Brokkr's, but no part of the neck might be cut. The court allowed it, and Brokkr took the price another way — he sewed Loki's lips together with the thread called Vartari. The episode ends there: the gods keep the treasures, Loki keeps his head, and Brokkr keeps the record of having made Mjǫllnir.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 35, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Grímnismál 43 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993), s.v. Brokk, Eitri, Sindri.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The smithing dwarf is native Germanic stock and needs no foreign original. The corpus keeps a guild of him: [[sindri|Sindri]] the sparkler, [[andvari|Andvari]] the gold-guardian, the sons of Ívaldi, and Vǫlundr of Vǫlundarkviða — 'prince of elves', smith of the heroic hoard, whose English cognate Wayland is named in Beowulf and pictured on the eighth-century Franks Casket. The dwarf-kennings of skaldic verse treat the whole tribe as the makers of every precious thing.[^1]

The comparison with the Greek smith-god Hēphaistos has been tried since the interpretatio romana paired Vulcan with the northern forge-figures, but the families differ where it matters: Hēphaistos is a god who makes wonders for gods, while Brokkr is a tradesman who beats the gods' own suppliers in open competition and collects on the debt. The sharpest contrast lives inside the corpus itself, between two dwarf-rings: Draupnir, made freely in a wager, drips eight rings every ninth night, while Andvari's ring, extorted under threat, kills every hand that holds it — the given ring multiplies, the taken ring devours.[^2]

Within the corpus, closely related figures include [[loki|Loki]] (the wager's loser), [[thor|Þórr]] (the hammer's owner), [[freyr|Freyr]] (the boar's), and [[svartalfaheimr|Svartálfaheimr]] (the world of the black-elves whose work the wager judged).

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. dwarfs, Brokk, Vǫlundr.
Orchard, Andy, Cassell's Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Brokk, dwarfs, Andvari.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Brokkr's afterlife is the afterlife of his hammer: every retelling of the Norse myths that shows Mjǫllnir made must walk back into his forge. The Victorian mythographies retold the wager as a set-piece of dwarf-craft, and every modern handbook keeps the episode as the founding legend of the gods' treasures.[^1]

Wagner's Ring rebuilt the dwarf-smith as Mime and Alberich — crossed with [[andvari|Andvari]]'s cursed gold — and Tolkien's dwarves, miners and master-smiths whose craft outlasts kingdoms, descend from the same þulur that list Brokkr's kin. Popular culture has since made the forge scene canonical: Marvel's Thor comics know both Brokk and Eitri as dwarf-smiths, and the films set the making of Thor's weapons in the dwarf-realm of Nidavellir — Snorri's episode retold for the largest audience the myth has ever had.[^1]

In Iceland the name itself survives as a rarity, and in the dictionaries as a word for a badger — the animal-name the smith may or may not have carried into myth. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú retellings keep the wager as the tradition's standing proof that craft, patiently kept, beats cunning every time it is tested.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Brokk, dwarfs, reception.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Brokkr is a purely literary figure: no runestone, votive deposit, or named image records him, and his name survives in the epigraphic record, if at all, only as raw anthroponymic material. His attestation is textual and, for an Eddic episode, unusually well witnessed: the wager stands in the principal codices of the Prose Edda — the Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to (c. 1300–1325) and its sister manuscripts — with the brother's name given as Eitri in the main text and Sindri in some copies.[^1]

The myth's material world, by contrast, is richly documented. The Mästermyr find from Gotland — a Viking-Age smith's complete tool chest buried about the year 1000 — preserves the bellows, hammers, tongs, and anvil of exactly the forge-culture the story presumes.[^2] And the wager's third casting left the deepest material trace of all: Thor's-hammer amulets, cast in silver and worn across the Viking world from the ninth century onward, are the archaeological footprint of Mjǫllnir — the smith's work carried at thousands of necks.

sources.citation: Faulkes, Anthony, ed., Edda: Prologue and Gylfaginning (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1982), on the manuscript transmission of the Prose Edda.
Arwidsson, Greta, and Gösta Berg, The Mästermyr Find: A Viking Age Tool Chest from Gotland (Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 1983).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic Edda never stages Brokkr's episode — the wager belongs to Snorri's prose — but the poems corroborate its foundations at both ends. Grímnismál 43 records the work of the rivals: 'Ívaldi's sons went in days of old to make Skíðblaðnir, best of ships, for bright Freyr' — the very benchmark Brokkr's three castings were judged against.[^1]

The Edda's dwarf-lore supplies the world around him. Vǫluspá's great catalogue of dwarfs, the Dvergatal, lists the smith-tribe by the score, and Vǫlundarkviða preserves the corpus's other great smith narrative — Vǫlundr, 'prince of elves', who forges in captivity and pays his debts in kind.[^2] The Þórr poems, finally, live on the wager's product: Mjǫllnir is the hammer of Þrymskviða and Hymiskviða, stolen and won back, swung against giants — every verse use of it a quiet footnote to the afternoon it came out of Brokkr's fire.[^3]

sources.citation: Grímnismál 43 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Vǫluspá (Dvergatal) and Vǫlundarkviða (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Þrymskviða and Hymiskviða (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The Prose Edda is Brokkr's only narrative witness, and it is a generous one. Skáldskaparmál 35 gives the fullest smithing episode in Old Norse: the cutting of Sif's hair, Loki's errand to the svartálfar, the sons of Ívaldi's three treasures, the wager of the head against Brokkr's brother — named Eitri in the main text, Sindri in some manuscripts — the three castings and the fly's three stings, the judgment of Óðinn, Þórr, and Freyr, and the closing scene in which Brokkr, denied the neck by the bargain's letter, sews Loki's lips together with the thread Vartari.[^1]

Snorri's craft deserves note: the episode exists to explain the kennings — why poets call gold 'Sif's hair' and the hammer by its dwarf-made fame — a myth doing the work of a dictionary, and doing it with a smith's eye for process. Gylfaginning adds the frame: the world of the svartálfar among the realms, and Draupnir's afterlife on Baldr's pyre, whence [[hermod|Hermóðr]] carries it back from Hel — the wager's second casting still circulating through the gods' greatest grief.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 35, trans. Faulkes (1987); Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993), s.v. Eitri, Sindri.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49 (Draupnir on Baldr's pyre), trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The runic corpus contains no attestation of the dwarf Brokkr. No runestone invokes him, no amulet bears his name, and the name does not appear among the securely read personal names of the inscriptions — a silence he shares with most of the mythological dwarfs, whose world was the forge of poetry rather than the cult of the carved stone.[^1]

What the runes can supply is the name's own rendering. In the sixteen-rune Younger Futhark, *Brokkr* would have been carved **ᛒᚱᚢᚴᛦ** (b-r-u-k-R): úr doing duty for the o the short row cannot write, the k-rune writing the geminate once, and ᛦ carrying the final nominative -r. The rendering is a normalized reconstruction, not an attestation — the primary witness remains the manuscript spelling of the Prose Edda, which is itself plain ASCII.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. dwarfs, Brokk.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), on the younger futhark.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond the Eddas, Brokkr's medieval afterlife is thin, and the record should say so plainly. The sagas of Icelanders and the kings' sagas do not stage him; his episode was Snorri's to tell, and no independent prose narrative retells the wager outside the Prose Edda's own manuscript family.[^1]

What the wider literature keeps is his kin and his products. The þulur — the metrical name-lists preserved with Skáldskaparmál — catalogue the dwarf-tribe among whom he stands, and skaldic verse runs on his afternoon's work: the kennings for poetry, gold, and battle presuppose dwarf-made treasures, and every hammer-kenning for Þórr's weapon is downstream of the forge-scene of Skáldskaparmál 35. The saga-age Icelanders who wrote of smiths and their craft — and the metalworkers whose tools the Mästermyr chest preserves — are the world the myth presumed; the myth's own testimony remains Snorri's.[^1][^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Brokk, dwarfs.
Arwidsson, Greta, and Gösta Berg, The Mästermyr Find: A Viking Age Tool Chest from Gotland (Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 1983).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Brokkr is the patron of the work that speaks for itself. He does not argue with the boast that the sons of Ívaldi cannot be matched; he takes the boast as a stake and makes three treasures in an afternoon. He is stung, and blows on. He is sabotaged at the last instant, and the flaw that results — a short handle — is the only thing the trickster ever wins from him; the Æsir judge the marred hammer best of all.[^1]

And when the bargain's letter is turned against him, he does not rage at the loophole: he honors it, and takes what the letter leaves. The corpus is full of oaths broken and bargains twisted, and against them all it sets this small, perfectly kept account — a smith who bet everything on his craft, lost nothing that mattered, and sewed shut, for a while, the mouth that thought skill was a bluff.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 35, trans. Faulkes (1987).
